figures.caption: Fig. 1. Delay-induced Hopf bifurcation in the Wilson–Cowan model for the “gentle” parameters of Table 1. (a) The equilibrium u∗ ≈ 0.186 (black) is stable for small delays and loses stability at a supercritical Hopf bifurcation at τc ≈ 0.108 (circle), giving rise to a branch of stable periodic orbits; blue curves show the maximum and minimum of u over one period. (b) Period T along the periodic branch. The orbit is born with the finite period 2π/ω ≈ 5.97, where ω ≈ 1.053 is the frequency of the critical characteristic roots, and the period then grows approximately linearly with τ .

Fig. 3. Floquet multipliers µ of the periodic orbits in Figure 2, just past each bifurcation; filled symbols lie outside the unit circle and the open symbol at µ = 1 is the trivial multiplier. (a) Antiphase orbit at τ = 0.0640: a complex pair has crossed the unit circle near µ ≈ −0.5 ± 0.87i (torus bifurcation), with argument close to ±2π/3. (b) Asymmetric orbit at τ = 0.2760: a real multiplier has passed through µ = −1 (period doubling).

Fig. 4. Representative periodic orbits for the “rich” parameters of Table 1. Top row: u(t) (coloured) and v(t) (grey) over two periods of the period-T orbit, with the equilibrium value u∗ dotted. Bottom row: projections onto the (u, v) plane, with the symmetry line u = v (dotted) and the equilibrium (dot). (a) Anti-phase orbit at τ = 0.055 (T = 0.219): one maximum per period and v(t) = u(t + T/2), so the projection is symmetric about u = v. (b) Asymmetric orbit at τ = 0.280 (T = 2.919): two maxima of different heights per period and no reflection symmetry. (c) Perioddoubled orbit at τ = 0.272 (period 2T , T = 2.854): successive maxima alternate in height, and the projection winds twice around a closed curve.

Fig. 5. Two-parameter bifurcation diagram in the plane of the cross-coupling b = c and the delay τ , with the remaining parameters as in Figure 2; the dotted vertical line marks the oneparameter slice b = 2.5 studied there. Hopf curves of the equilibrium are computed analytically for the anti-phase (solid) and in-phase (dash-dot) modes; the equilibrium is stable in the shaded region, and the curves intersect at double Hopf points (dots). The torus curve (purple) and the perioddoubling curve (green) were obtained by numerical continuation with DDE-BIFTOOL. Stars mark points on the torus curve where the rotation number is rational (i.e. points of mode locking).

Fig. 6. Route to chaos through torus breakdown as the delay is increased, for the “rich” parameters of Table 1. (a) Orbit diagram: local maxima of u(t) after transients, computed by direct simulation from a single initial history for each τ . (b) Largest Lyapunov exponent λmax. The equilibrium loses stability at the Hopf bifurcation τH ≈ 0.0486, and the resulting anti-phase orbit undergoes a torus bifurcation at τT ≈ 0.064, after which the maxima fill an interval and λmax ≈ 0 (quasi-periodic motion). Windows of mode locking follow, and from τC ≈ 0.0755 the exponent becomes clearly positive (chaos).

Fig. 7. Solutions along the route to chaos in Figure 6. Top row: u(t) (blue) and v(t) (grey) over a short time window. Middle row: projection onto the (u, v) plane. Bottom row: return map of successive maxima of u. (a) Periodic anti-phase orbit, τ = 0.060: a single fixed point of the return map. (b) Quasi-periodic solution after the torus bifurcation, τ = 0.068: the return map traces a closed invariant curve. (c) Mode-locked solution, τ = 0.0735: the invariant curve is replaced by a periodic orbit, seen as a finite set of points. (d) Chaotic solution, τ = 0.1: the invariant curve has broken up and the return map fills a folded set.
